description: We are Team ALAZ, a duo studying Space & Astronomy Sciences and Computer Engineering. We're tackling the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge to build a unified wildfire tracking system. We combine scientific precision with strong technical execution. We need 2 teammates skilled in Data Science (Python), GIS, Web Dev, UI/UX, or Storytelling to help build our prototype. Join us to turn NASA satellite data into a real-world climate solution!
summary: For 25 years, NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites have recorded every active fire on Earth, but they count differently: VIIRS sees fires about ten times smaller, so raw hotspot counts jump whenever a new satellite joins, even when nothing changed on the ground. ALAZ Relay fixes the record itself. Using the ten years when Aqua MODIS and VIIRS flew together, it learns how often MODIS would have seen each VIIRS fire, and rebuilds one consistent, Aqua-equivalent fire record from 2000 to today for the whole planet on a 0.1° grid, so the record continues after MODIS retires. Tested on years it never saw, it reproduces real Aqua with r = 0.99. A free web app lets anyone draw an area or pick a country and read its burning activity calendar: fire seasons, anomalies, record months and honest uncertainty, downloadable as CSV. The harmonized record changes the story: raw hotspots say global fire rose six-fold after 2012; in one consistent unit it fell about 11%, matching independent evidence.
details:
What it does

ALAZ Relay is a harmonized, global, 25-year active-fire record, together with a web app for reading it.

  • One unit across all sensors. Every hotspot from Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 is converted into fire cell-days: a 0.1° grid cell counts once per day and overpass when it burns, however many pixels lit up. This removes most of the resolution effect before any modelling.
  • Virtual MODIS from VIIRS. For every VIIRS fire cell-day we estimate the probability that Aqua MODIS would also have detected it, based on the fire's radiative power, its size in VIIRS pixels, day or night, and the country. We then add the share of fires that Aqua sees and VIIRS misses (cloud, timing, swath gaps). The sum is a "virtual Aqua": what Aqua would have reported.
  • A relay, decided day by day. Before Aqua existed (Nov 2000 – Jul 2002), Terra is converted to Aqua-equivalent units. From Aug 2002 to Dec 2011, real Aqua is the record. From 2012 on, virtual Aqua comes from Suomi NPP and NOAA-20, averaged on days when both deliver data. If one satellite has an outage (Suomi NPP in Jul–Aug 2022 and Jul 2024), the other carries that day. Suomi NPP's FIRMS stream ended in November 2026; because NOAA-20 has its own independently trained model, the relay can continue on NOAA-20 alone.
  • Burning activity calendar. For any area, the app shows a year-by-month calendar in three views: harmonized activity, anomaly against the 2003–2022 median, and raw hotspots for comparison. It also reports the peak season, the most active year, and how much of the apparent trend was only a sensor change. A month is flagged as an anomaly only when the low end of its 90% uncertainty interval is above the historical upper quartile, and as a record when it is above every month in the baseline.
  • Accessible and open. Colour ramps are perceptually ordered and readable in dark mode. Areas can be drawn as rectangles or polygons, entered as latitude/longitude plus a radius, or chosen as a country. Every result downloads as CSV. The site is fully static (no server, no API key), so anyone can host or reuse it.

What the record reveals

  • Global fire went down, not up. With yearly global totals indexed to 2003–2011 = 100, raw hotspots (summed the way most fire maps do) jump to 485 in 2012, when Suomi NPP joins, and to 688–895 from 2018, when NOAA-20 joins: ×6.1 on average over 2012–2022. ALAZ Relay gives 88.5 for the same years (−11.5%). Aqua MODIS alone, a single unchanged sensor that we never adjusted, gives 89.0 (−11%). The decline matches published evidence that global burned area is falling, mostly in savannas (Andela et al., 2017).
  • It finds disasters on its own. For every country and calendar month since 2012, we test whether that month is higher than the same month in every other year since 2001 (leave-one-out). 516 months are the highest on record; for 45 of them, even the low end of the 90% uncertainty interval beats every other year. The detector is never told about any event, yet it finds Canada's record 2023 season (June 2023, 8.9× a normal June), Sweden's 2018 forest fires (11.6×), Chile's Biobío and Ñuble megafires (February 2023, 8.4×), the Riau peat fires (March 2014, 6.1×) and the Corrientes wetland fires (January 2022, 4.9×). It is also honest about what it cannot separate: Australia's Black Summer (December 2019) and the 2020 US West Coast fires are the highest months since 2001, but stay within the uncertainty band at national scale.
  • Why you draw areas. At country level, Türkiye's August 2021 ranks only 17th of 25 Augusts, because crop-stubble burning in the southeast dominates the national total. Draw the area around Manavgat, and July–August 2021 becomes the record by a wide margin.

How we know it works

  • Held-out validation. Trained on 2012–2017, the model predicted Aqua for 2018–2021 from Suomi NPP alone. Across 3,965 country-months worldwide: r (log) = 0.987, bias +2.8%, median error 15%. NOAA-20, trained only on 2018–2019 and tested on 2020–2021: r = 0.986, bias +3.5%, median error 15%. The remaining error becomes the uncertainty band shown on every month.
  • The baton test. The two VIIRS satellites are trained independently, so their two virtual Aquas must agree if the method is sound. They do: r = 0.997, with a median gap of −1.2% over 7,616 country-months (2018–2025).
  • An independent ground check (illustrative). Manavgat 2021 vs. 2008 (Jul–Aug, same area): raw hotspots 30×, ALAZ Relay 4.2×, mapped burned area 3.4–3.8×.
  • Honest limits. Fire cell-days measure how often fire is seen, not hectares burned. From 2022 both Terra and Aqua drift to later overpass times, so post-2021 Aqua is used only as a check, not as a reference. FIRMS static land sources (gas flares, industry, volcanoes) are removed: they make up 27% of VIIRS hotspots in Türkiye, against 2.8% for MODIS.

Benefits

  • Fire services and planners can see whether a season is truly unusual for their district, not merely unusual for a new satellite.
  • Researchers and journalists get one continuous 25-year series instead of three incompatible ones.
  • The method keeps working after MODIS ends (Terra and Aqua science operations are planned to end in 2027). Without a bridge like this, the longest satellite fire record on Earth would break in two.

What we hope to achieve

We want the next fire spike that makes the news to be checked against a record that does not change when the satellites do. Next steps: add NOAA-21 to the relay, extend the record through 2026 with FIRMS near-real-time data, publish the gridded product as an open dataset, and strengthen the ground truth by comparing with burned-area products region by region.

Tools and technology

  • Pipeline: Python 3.11, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy and PyArrow, processing 548.5 million FIRMS records into 32 million harmonized cell-months.
  • Web app: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with MapLibre GL JS, D3.js and topojson-client. Compact binary tiles (65 MB for the whole planet) are decoded in the browser.
  • Demo video: animated in Remotion (React) from our own data, plus a screen recording of the live app made with Playwright. The voiceover is an AI voice generated with ElevenLabs from our script. Music and sound effects are synthesized in Python (NumPy/SciPy), so no copyrighted audio is used.
